I read your email to the investors. The content is excellent, but some sentences are very long.
I know. In Portuguese, a long sentence sounds intelligent. In English, it sounds wordy.
Exactly. Your second paragraph is one run-on sentence. Try to cut it into three.
Okay. But how do I connect the three sentences? Should I repeat the decision every time?
No. Say this decision once, then use moreover for the next point. That way the text will flow.
That makes sense. And the subject line? I just wrote Information.
That tells them nothing. Put the takeaway there: Tariff decision, no impact on returns.
Perfect. I will rewrite it now, and then could you proofread it before lunch?

Let me put the takeaway in the subject line.

I edit a law journal, and I read papers from all over the world. The ideas are usually excellent. The most common problem is not grammar. It is sentences that are too long. A reader in English expects one idea per sentence and one main idea per paragraph. My second piece of advice is about the word this. Many authors start a sentence with this, alone, and the reader does not know what it refers to. This decision, this approach, this problem: add the noun, and the reader never gets lost. Finally, read your text out loud. If you need to breathe in the middle of a sentence, the sentence is too long.

When I arrived in New York, I wrote like a Brazilian judge. Some of my sentences were eighty words long, with three or four ideas inside. I thought that was elegant. My first memo came back from my partner with one comment, in red: too long, where is the takeaway? I was a bit offended. But she was right. American clients read on their phones, between meetings. Now my rule is simple. The takeaway goes in the first sentence. Each sentence has one idea. And I connect them with small words: this, moreover, in addition. My memos are shorter now, and clients actually answer them.

How do busy professionals read their email? A communication company studied the inboxes of two thousand office workers, and the answer is: very fast. The average professional receives more than one hundred emails a day. Most people read only the subject line and the first sentence before they decide to open an email or not. Emails with long paragraphs are much less likely to get an answer. The researchers' advice is simple. Put the main point in the subject line, use short sentences and bullet points, and proofread before you send. Your reader is busy, and the first ten seconds decide everything.
